story.title: Built on 27 million files and a drawer of old drives.
story.p1: BackDown began as a one-off job: consolidate years of old disks onto one archive and wipe the rest. The hard part was never copying bytes.
story.p2: Five of six drives held generations of the same data. The most valuable thing on them, a mail server's archive, only turned up by reading the shell script that once backed it up. And 5.9 TB of the biggest drive was quietly duplicating itself.
story.p3: No backup tool would have told us any of that. So we built one that does.
story.s1_label: files indexed, with every job resumable when a USB drive dropped off the bus
story.s2_label: of storage read and hashed, with source drives mounted read-only throughout
story.s3_label: of the biggest drive found duplicating itself
story.s4_label: drives wiped, each only after every byte was hash-verified elsewhere
how.title: Plug in everything. Get answers, not a vault.
how.intro: Backup tools answer "can I restore this file?" BackDown also answers "what do I have, what's duplicated, and what's safe to delete?"
how.s1_title: Point it at every drive you own
how.s1_body: Old laptops, NAS shares, the USB disk in the drawer. Sources are mounted read-only and tracked by serial number, never by /dev/sdX, so the wrong disk is never touched.
how.s2_body: Tiered hashing checks size first, then a quick sample, then a full SHA-256, so it only fully reads files that could be duplicates. If a drive disconnects or the machine reboots, you lose the file in flight, not the night.
how.s3_title: You get a verdict for every drive
how.s3_body: What's on it, what each folder is, what's duplicated across every source, and a verdict: safe to wipe, or copy these 212 GB first. Nothing is deleted without a verified copy.
features.title: The intelligence other backup tools leave out.
features.intro: Borg, restic and Time Machine are excellent vaults. BackDown adds the layer that tells you what you're actually storing.
features.legend: BackDown is pre-release, so each feature is marked with its status.
features.f1_body: Not just inside one repository. Each new drive is checked against everything already indexed. Hardlinks and symlinks are accounted for, so reclaim figures are real.
features.f2_title: Proof a drive is safe to wipe
features.f2_body: Either every file has a SHA-256-identical copy elsewhere, or you get the list of files that don't. Every copy and deletion is journaled against a verified hash.
features.f3_body: Every long job resumes where it stopped. Flaky USB enclosures are remounted automatically, and jobs run one per spindle so a single disk never thrashes.
features.f4_body: Maildirs, Time Machine sets, phone backups, home directories, disk images, git repos, SQL dumps and cloud exports, each with a date range and size. Regenerable caches are flagged, and can be left out.
features.f5_body: BackDown reads the rsync scripts, sync markers and backup metadata that record your data's history. It can say "rsynced from your mail server on 31 May 2020," not just "some files."
features.f6_title: A web UI you'll actually open
features.f6_body: Live progress, interactive size trees, duplicate tables and per-drive verdicts, served locally by the daemon, in light and dark.
features.f7_body: Mailboxes appear as threaded mail, photos as a gallery, SQL dumps as schemas. Disk images open read-only, no mounting needed. Search every backup and drive at once.
features.f8_body: Content-defined chunking, zstd compression and client-side encryption, verified on a schedule, to local disks, SFTP, S3 or B2.
features.f9_body: Signed, append-only manifests of every copy, move and delete, a record you can hand to an auditor or a court.
privacy.title: Your data stays on your disks.
privacy.intro: Most backup services start by uploading everything. BackDown starts from the opposite end.
privacy.p1_body: The local edition makes no network requests. It needs no account and sends no telemetry.
privacy.p2_body: Drives being analysed are mounted read-only, so a flaky enclosure can't corrupt the data you're trying to save.
privacy.p3_body: Nothing is removed unless a copy with a matching hash is already in the journal.
privacy.p4_body: The optional team dashboard sees metadata only. Your files leave your machines only if you add a cloud backup target.

features.f10_body: Every scan is kept, so the file browser can show any folder as it was on any scan date, with previews and read-only viewers for PDFs, office documents, SQLite databases, git history and diffs.
features.f11_body: After the first scan, BackDown asks the drive's own change log what's changed: the FSEvents history on macOS or the USN journal on Windows, even after the drive was unplugged. On NTFS drives it can also read the master file table directly, listing millions of files in seconds. Anything the log can't vouch for is scanned in full, so nothing is missed. Free in every edition.
faq.title: Pricing questions

faq.a2: One seat covers one computer running BackDown, however many drives or terabytes it looks at. You're never charged for the amount of data.
faq.a3: No. The local edition needs no account and makes no network requests. A licence is a signed key you add once; BackDown checks it offline.

start.title: From download to your first verdict in five minutes.
start.intro: BackDown only ever reads your drives. The index lives in your own data folder, and nothing leaves your machine.
start.s1_body: Unpack the archive and move backdown somewhere on your path. On Windows, unzip it and run backdown.exe from a terminal.
start.s2_body: Point it at every drive or folder you want to understand. Each run is a scan you can come back to.
start.s3_body: dupes lists what's duplicated, biggest first. check says whether a drive is safe to wipe: it exits with 0 when every file has a verified copy elsewhere.
start.s4_body: Opens the file browser in your web browser: every folder at any scan, with previews, copies and versions.
start.s5_body: Installs a systemd service that rescans drives when they're due or plugged back in, and keeps the browser a click away.
verify.title: Every file has a checksum.
verify.body: Download SHA256SUMS.txt from the release page next to your archive, then check it. Preview builds aren't signed yet, so this is how you know the file is ours.

status.principle1: Never write to a source drive. Drives being analysed are only ever read.
status.principle2: Never delete without a verified copy. Every deletion is backed by a matching hash in the journal.
status.principle3: Every long job can resume, and shows you why it's slow.
status.principle4: The free tier answers "what do I have, and what's duplicated?" completely.
status.principle5: Local first. No account, no telemetry, and no cloud needed for anything in the core.
policy.title: Privacy policy
policy.intro: This covers the website, backdown.io. The BackDown app itself makes no network requests and sends nothing to us.
policy.waitlist_body: If you join, we store your email address and the language of the page you signed up on. We use them to send you one email when BackDown is ready, and for nothing else. We never share or sell your address, and we delete it on request.
policy.analytics_on: We count visits with Matomo, running on our own server. It sets no cookies, doesn't follow you to other sites, and the numbers aren't shared with anyone. If your browser sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control, the counting script isn't loaded at all.
policy.analytics_off: This site doesn't use analytics or trackers of any kind.
policy.orders_body: Payments are handled by Stripe; we never see your card number. For each order we keep your name, email address, billing country and address (to calculate tax), what you bought, and the licence key we issued, for as long as tax law requires. Stripe's privacy policy covers what Stripe does.
policy.hosting_body: The site is served by Cloudflare, which processes technical data such as IP addresses to deliver the pages and protect them from abuse.
policy.rights_body: You can ask what we hold about you, and have it corrected or deleted, at any time. If you're in the EU or UK, you can also complain to your data protection authority.
